newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mobutu "nephew" unauthorised to talk - Mobutu aide.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu "nephew" unauthorised to talk - Mobutu aide.

text.p: The Zairean envoy who met South African President Nelson Mandela as part of a campaign to end a rebel uprising is unauthorised to talk on behalf of President Mobutu Sese Seko, Mobutu's spokesman said on Thursday.
"He has no authority to do that kind of thing," the spokesman told Reuters, referring to Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, who met Mandela in Pretoria for an hour of talks on Thursday.

"He is in South Africa for personal reasons. He was in no way sent there to negotiate," the spokesman said in a telephone interview, insisting that Mobutu will not agree to negotiations until all foreign soldiers have withdrawn from Zairean soil.
Zaire's president of 31 years is currently at his villa in southern France while recuperating from prostate cancer surgery and radiation treatments carried out last year in Switzerland.
The spokesman said Mobutu would leave France to return to Zaire later this week.

South African President Nelson Mandela, launching a diplomatic initative to end a rebel uprising in eastern Zaire, said on Thursday progress had been made in his separate talks with Zaire's warring parties but kept the details to himself.
Mandela met Ngbanda, widely identified as Mobutu's nephew, a day after talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila in attempts to get the two sides in roundtable talks and hopefully broker a truce.
Mobutu's spokesman confirmed Ngbanda was an "adviser" to the Zairean head of state but denied he was the president's nephew.
He said Ngbanda had been in South Africa for personal reasons and was grabbed by South African and U.S. officials as well as the news media "simply because he was on the spot. It was an accident".
In Pretoria earlier on Thursday, Mandela said Ngbanda "appreciates the importance of peace in Zaire and that this peace will only be brought about by negotiations with Laurent Kabila".

Asked if direct talks were now a possibility, Ngbanda said only: "That is part of our discussions." He said he had met U.S. officials and that Mobutu was committed to a peaceful settlement, but one that must "respect Zaire's territorial sovereignty".
Zaire, which has employed foreign mercenaries to bolster its army, accuses Uganda and Tutsi-led Rwanda and Burundi of fighting with the rebels, many of whom are also ethnic Tutsis.
Zaire's three eastern neighbours deny involvement in the conflict, which has sent tens of thousands of local people and Hutu refugees fleeing from Rwanda and Burundi.
